title: Add NetworkError and tighten retry logic
summary: Ky now wraps a recognized fetch network failure in a typed `NetworkError`. By default it retries only the errors it knows, and throws every other error at once.

links.title: Best way to handle Fetch errors such as Failed to fetch (#545)
PR comment: why inline the dependency
PR comment: not worth a compile step

steps.title: Fetch errors are vague
steps.body:
When the network fails, `fetch` rejects with a plain `TypeError`. The message depends on the runtime:
- Chrome: `Failed to fetch`
- Node.js: `fetch failed`
- Safari 17+: `Load failed`

A bug can also throw a `TypeError`, such as `Cannot read properties of undefined`. Before this PR, Ky did not wrap either kind of `TypeError`. The caller and the retry logic got the same type for both.

steps.title: Ky retried unknown errors too
steps.body:
Before this PR, the retry logic knew two error types:
- An `HTTPError` retried by its status code.
- A `TimeoutError` retried only when `retryOnTimeout` was on.
- Every other error fell through to a retry, bugs included.

Issue #545 asked how to retry only real network errors.

steps.title: Wrap known errors, retry known types
steps.body:
In #545, sholladay proposed two changes. sindresorhus approved both.
- Wrap a known network error from `fetch` in a new `NetworkError`. The original error stays at `cause`.
- Retry only the error types that Ky knows: `HTTPError`, `TimeoutError` and `NetworkError`. Throw any other error at once.

A network error from a runtime that Ky does not know now fails without a retry. sindresorhus accepted this cost: "New runtimes don't come along every day." A `shouldRetry` callback can still force a retry of any error.

steps.title: Why the detector is inlined
steps.body:
The PR copies the detector from the `is-network-error` package, v1.3.1, into `source/utils/is-network-error.ts`. Ky gets no new dependency.

sholladay called the copy "a bit silly", because Ky already has a compile step. sindresorhus answered that compiling a dependency is "not worth the effort for a single one that won't update very often".

The copy is named `isRawNetworkError`. The public name `isNetworkError` then means "is a Ky `NetworkError`", like `isHTTPError` and `isTimeoutError`.

steps.title: A breaking change
steps.body: The v2.0.0 release notes list this PR under "Breaking": "Add `NetworkError` class and tighten retry logic (#842)". It first shipped in v2.0.0-0. At the PR commit, `package.json` still says 1.14.3.

steps.title: Ky in five facts
steps.body:
- Ky is an HTTP client that calls `fetch`: the runtime's own, or the one in the `fetch` option.
- Each call, such as `ky.get(url)`, creates one `Ky` instance for that request.
- When an attempt fails, the retry decision gets the error. It returns a wait, or it throws the error to stop.
- Before the next attempt, Ky waits for a backoff that grows with each retry.
- Hooks let app code see each retry (`beforeRetry`) and each final error (`beforeError`).

steps.title: Errors from fetch
steps.say: When `fetch` rejects, Ky first checks what kind of error it got.

terms.meaning: The set of exact messages that runtimes put on a network `TypeError`, such as `fetch failed` from Node.js. It holds 8 messages from Chrome, Firefox, Safari 16, Node.js, Bun, Cloudflare Workers and `cross-fetch`.
A `TypeError` from `fetch` that `isRawNetworkError` recognizes as a network failure. Its message is on the runtime message list, or it matches a Chrome, Deno or Safari 17 form.
The standard `Error` property that holds the error behind this one. When Ky wraps a raw network error, it keeps the original at `cause`.

steps.title: Ky's error types
steps.say: Ky now wraps a raw network error in its own type, as it already did for HTTP and timeout failures.

terms.meaning: The base class of Ky's own errors. The error types below extend it.
The error that Ky throws by default when the response status is not 2xx. It holds the `response` and the `request`.
The error that Ky throws when a request runs past its `timeout`, 10 s by default. The time counts across all attempts of the request.
The new error for a request that got no response, such as after a DNS failure or a refused connection. It holds the `request` and keeps the raw network error at `cause`.
The public check for a `NetworkError`. It is true for an instance of `NetworkError` or for any error whose `name` is `'NetworkError'`.

steps.title: The retry decision
steps.say: After a failed attempt, the retry decision reads the error and chooses to wait and retry, or to stop.

terms.meaning: The private `Ky` method that gets the error of a failed attempt. It returns the wait before the next attempt, or throws the error to stop retrying.
The most retries after the first attempt, 2 by default. So a request makes at most 3 attempts.
The HTTP methods that Ky retries: by default GET, PUT, HEAD, DELETE, OPTIONS and TRACE. POST and PATCH are not in the default list.
A user callback that runs after the limit and method checks. It can force a retry (`true`), stop (`false`), or leave the choice to the default rules (`undefined`).
The wait before a retry, from `retry.delay`. By default it starts at 0.3 s and doubles for each retry.
App callbacks that run after the backoff, before the next attempt. Each one gets the `error` and the `retryCount`.
App callbacks that get the final `error` before Ky rejects the request. A hook may return a different error for Ky to throw.

steps.title: Which errors Ky retries
steps.say: Which errors does Ky retry after this PR? With no `shouldRetry` callback, the error type decides, once the retry limit and the request method allow a retry.

notes.text: A failed attempt starts at one of three sources: a non-ok response, the timeout timer, or a `fetch` rejection.
A non-ok response becomes an `HTTPError`. The timer rejects with a `TimeoutError`. This PR keeps both errors as they were.

`Ky#fetch` now checks each `fetch` rejection for a raw network error. That is a `TypeError` with a message from the runtime message list, such as `Failed to fetch`. A match becomes a `NetworkError` that keeps the original error at `cause`.
Any other rejection keeps its own type and message. A `TypeError` from a bug, such as `Cannot read properties of undefined`, stays a plain `TypeError`.
An `HTTPError` retries when its status is in `retry.statusCodes`, such as 503. A `TimeoutError` retries only when `retryOnTimeout` is true. A `NetworkError` retries with no extra option.
Any other error goes to the app after the first attempt, with its type and message unchanged. An `HTTPError` or a `TimeoutError` that fails its rule goes to the app too.

steps.title: A custom fetch that throws
steps.question: With default options, a custom `fetch` throws `new Error('boom')` on a GET: how many `fetch` calls happen, and what does the app get?

options.text: One call, and the app gets the same `Error('boom')`.
options.why: The error is not a `TypeError` with a known message, so the retry decision throws it on the first attempt.

options.text: Three calls, and the app gets `Error('boom')` after two retries.
options.why: Before this PR, an unknown error retried up to the default `retry.limit` of 2.

options.text: One call, and the app gets a `NetworkError` with `Error('boom')` at `cause`.
options.why: Only a `TypeError` with a message from the runtime message list becomes a `NetworkError`.

options.text: Three calls, and the app gets a `NetworkError` after two retries.
options.why: `Ky#fetch` never wraps `Error('boom')`, so no `NetworkError` exists to retry.

steps.title: Wrap and retry a failed fetch
steps.say: In this flow, the first fetch of `ky.get(url)` fails on the network. `#fetch` now wraps that failure in a `NetworkError`. The retry decision retries the `NetworkError` after a backoff.

messages.label: ky.get(url)
messages.note: The `get` shortcut merges the instance defaults with the call's options and passes them to `Ky.create`.

messages.label: #retry(() => #fetch())
messages.note: `Ky.create` starts the first attempt by passing `#fetch` to `#retry`.

messages.label: #fetch()
messages.note: When `retry.limit` is above 0, `#fetch` keeps a clone of the request for the next attempt.

messages.label: await timeout(...)
messages.note: The call now runs inside a `try` with `await`, so a rejection reaches the `catch` of `#fetch`.

messages.label: options.fetch(request, init)
messages.note: `timeout` starts the runtime `fetch` and a timer at the same time.

messages.label: TypeError: Failed to fetch
messages.note: The runtime rejects with a plain `TypeError` that carries Chrome's message.

messages.label: rejection, timer cleared
messages.note: `timeout` passes the same `TypeError` on and clears its timer.

messages.label: throw new NetworkError(...)
messages.note: The `catch` knows the message and throws a `NetworkError` with the `TypeError` at `cause`.

messages.label: #retryFromError(error)
messages.note: The unchanged `catch` in `#retry` sends every failure to `#retryFromError`.

messages.label: #calculateRetryDelay(error)
messages.note: `#retryFromError` asks the retry decision how long to wait, or whether to stop.

messages.label: backoff delay
messages.note: A `NetworkError` gets the default backoff, 300 ms before the first retry.

messages.label: beforeRetry({error, retryCount})
messages.note: After the wait, each `beforeRetry` hook gets the `NetworkError` with `retryCount` 1.

messages.label: #retry(fn), second attempt
messages.note: `#retryFromError` adds 1 to `#retryCount` and calls `#retry` again.

messages.label: Response
messages.note: The `Response` of the second fetch returns up through each nested `#retry` call.

messages.label: Response
messages.note: The `Response` passes the `afterResponse` hooks and the `throwHttpErrors` check on its way to the app.

steps.title: One try covers both fetch paths
steps.say: `#fetch` now awaits both fetch paths inside one `try`. So its new `catch` sees every rejection of the runtime `fetch`.

notes.text: Before, `#fetch` returned each fetch promise without `await` or `try`. The runtime's `TypeError` went straight to the `catch` in `#retry`.
With `timeout: false`, `#fetch` calls `options.fetch` directly. The added `await` lets the `catch` below see this rejection. A bare `return` of the promise would skip the `catch`.
With `timeout: false`, a custom `fetch` that throws `Failed to fetch` still gives the caller a `NetworkError`.
Otherwise `timeout`, Ky's helper that races `options.fetch` against a timer, runs under `await` too. A spent total timeout throws `TimeoutError` before any fetch starts.
Any other error leaves the `catch` as it is. A `TimeoutError` and a bug's `TypeError` keep their type and message.
A `TypeError` with the message `Cannot read properties of undefined` reaches the caller unwrapped.

steps.title: A known failure becomes NetworkError
steps.say: The new `catch` wraps a rejection in a `NetworkError` only when `isRawNetworkError` knows its message.

notes.text: The `catch` first asks `isRawNetworkError`, the check copied from `is-network-error` v1.3.1. It is true only for a `TypeError` with a known runtime message.
Safari 17+ uses the generic message `Load failed`. It counts only when the error has no stack, or when Sentry marked it with `__sentry_captured__`.
Chrome's `Failed to fetch` and Deno's messages have their own checks above. Every other message needs an exact match in `errorMessages`. A message that differs by one character does not match.
`errorMessages` holds the exact texts from Chrome, Firefox, Safari 16, `cross-fetch`, Node's undici, Bun and Cloudflare Workers. Undici has two entries: `fetch failed` and `terminated`.
A match becomes a `NetworkError` for `this.request`, the same request a `TimeoutError` gets. The runtime's `TypeError` stays at `cause`.
`NetworkError` extends `KyError` and sets `name` to `'NetworkError'`. Its message names the method and the URL: `Request failed due to a network error: GET https://example.com/`.
`isKyError`, the public check for any Ky error, now also checks for a `NetworkError`.
With `retry: 0`, a custom `fetch` that throws `TypeError('Failed to fetch')` gives the caller a `NetworkError`. The test checks its `request`, the `TypeError` at `cause`, and `isKyError`.

steps.title: Retry only the known error types
steps.say: The retry decision, `#calculateRetryDelay`, first runs its unchanged gates in order: the retry limit, `ForceRetryError`, the retriable methods, then `shouldRetry`. Past those gates, only an `HTTPError`, a `TimeoutError` or a `NetworkError` can get a delay.

notes.text: Before, the timeout branch only threw. A `TimeoutError` with `retryOnTimeout` on fell through to the shared backoff at the end.
`retry.retryOnTimeout` is the option that lets a `TimeoutError` retry. It is `false` by default. When it is `true`, the branch now returns the backoff itself.
The HTTP branch now returns its backoff too. Before, a retriable status left the branch and reached the shared backoff at the end.

The new guard throws every error that is not a `NetworkError`, such as a bug's `TypeError` or a plain `Error`. Before, these errors fell through to the backoff and retried. Now only a `NetworkError` reaches the last line.
`isNetworkError` is true for an `instanceof NetworkError`, or for any error whose `name` is `'NetworkError'`.
With `retry.limit` 2, a `TypeError` with an unknown message now stops after one fetch call.
A `NetworkError` still retries. After two `Failed to fetch` rejections, the third fetch returns `ok`.

steps.title: Trace one network retry
steps.question: A GET fails once with `TypeError: fetch failed`, then succeeds: what does the app get, and what does the `beforeRetry` hook see?

options.text: The app gets the `Response`. The hook sees a `NetworkError` with the `TypeError` at `cause`.
options.why: `fetch failed` is in `errorMessages`, so the retry decision gets a `NetworkError` and returns the backoff.

options.text: The app gets the `Response`. The hook sees the raw `TypeError` with the message `fetch failed`.
options.why: `#fetch` wraps the `TypeError` before `#retry` gets it, so no hook sees the raw error.

options.text: The app gets a `NetworkError`. The hook never runs, because Ky no longer retries a `TypeError`.
options.why: The guard throws only errors that are not a `NetworkError`, and `#fetch` already turned this `TypeError` into one.

options.text: The app gets the raw `TypeError`. The hook never runs, because Node's message is not on the list.
options.why: `errorMessages` lists `fetch failed` for undici, the `fetch` in Node.

steps.title: An unknown error fails at once
steps.say: Here the rejection is not a raw network error, such as a bug's `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined`. Ky now throws it to the app after one fetch call.

messages.label: rethrow the original error
messages.note: `isRawNetworkError` does not know the message, so the `catch` rethrows the error as it is.

messages.label: #retryFromError(error)
messages.note: `#retry` hands the error on, as it does for every failure.

messages.label: #calculateRetryDelay(error)
messages.note: The retry decision gets the plain `TypeError`.

messages.label: throw error
messages.note: The new guard throws the `TypeError` because it is not a `NetworkError`.

messages.label: throw
messages.note: The `result` wrapper in `Ky.create` catches the error and runs any `beforeError` hooks.

messages.label: reject with original error
messages.note: The app gets the same `TypeError`, not a `NetworkError`, after one fetch call.

steps.title: The last NetworkError reaches the app
steps.say: Here every fetch fails with a network error. Once the retry limit is reached, the retry decision throws the `NetworkError` instead of a delay. A POST takes this path on its first failure, because POST is not a retriable method.

messages.label: throw NetworkError
messages.note: The limit check runs first and throws the last `NetworkError`, after 2 retries by default.

messages.label: throw
messages.note: The error passes up through each nested `#retry` call to the `result` wrapper.

messages.label: beforeError({error, retryCount})
messages.note: Each `beforeError` hook gets the `NetworkError`, with `retryCount` 2 after two retries.

messages.label: error
messages.note: Only a returned `Error` replaces the error that the app gets.

messages.label: reject with NetworkError
messages.note: The runtime's `TypeError` is at `cause`, so an undici error code now sits at `error.cause.cause.code`.

steps.title: Where the classification may be wrong
steps.body:
`isRawNetworkError` classifies an error by its message only. Check these cases before approval.

- Undici's `fetch failed` also wraps an invalid URL scheme (`test/memory-leak.ts:40`) and a content-length mismatch (`test/headers.ts:127-143`). Both now become a `NetworkError`. Ky retries them when the method is retriable. The comment at `source/core/Ky.ts:485` promises that Ky does not retry programming bugs.
- Ky wraps only a rejection of the fetch call. A network failure while `.json()` or `.text()` reads the body (`source/core/Ky.ts:226-246`) stays a raw `TypeError`. Ky does not retry it.
- `isNetworkError` also accepts any error whose `name` is `NetworkError`. A `DOMException` with that name passes the check. `isKyError` accepts it too. Ky then retries it. TypeScript narrows it to a Ky `NetworkError`, although the `DOMException` has no `request`.
- The message list holds exact English strings. If a runtime changes its wording, Ky stops wrapping and retrying that error without a warning. The copy is pinned to `is-network-error` v1.3.1. Nothing keeps it in sync with the package.

steps.title: Who loses retries or breaks
steps.body:
A network failure now reaches the caller as a Ky `NetworkError`. Code that inspects the raw error, or that relied on the old retries, must change.

- A check on `instanceof TypeError` or on `error.message === 'Failed to fetch'` no longer matches a network failure. The runtime error now sits at `error.cause`.
- Code that reads undici's `error.cause.code` no longer finds it. The code is now one level deeper, at `error.cause.cause.code` (`test/headers.ts:142-143`).
- #545 accepted that unknown runtimes lose retries. A custom `fetch` or wrapper that throws its own error, such as a plain `Error`, loses them too. Before, Ky retried that error. Now the caller gets it after the first attempt.
- The #545 workaround turns retries off. Its `beforeRetry` hook throws when `isNetworkError` from the `is-network-error` package returns false. That function accepts only a `TypeError` (see its copy at `source/utils/is-network-error.ts:21`). The hook now gets a Ky `NetworkError`, so it throws on every network error.
- Ky's new `isNetworkError` export has the same name as the package function. It checks for a Ky `NetworkError` instead.
- Neither the PR nor the v2.0.0 release notes name these migration steps.
